Here are the verse-by-verse notes, compiled exclusively from the sources searched and fetched:

## John 19:22-42 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 22 — “What I have written, I have written.”

Pilate’s reply is a formula of finality. **Gill** notes it is a common rabbinical idiom meaning what is done stands irrevocable, and adds that Pilate was “over ruled by divine providence” so that the inscription remained — a kind of unwitting prophecy that the Jews would have no king but Jesus.

**Ellicott** explains the chief priests wanted the wording changed from “The King of the Jews” to “He said, I am King of the Jews,” but Pilate refused in order to humiliate them. The inscription in three languages (Hebrew, Greek, Latin) ensured that many read it.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/19.htm
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html

---

### v. 23 — Soldiers divide His garments; the seamless tunic.

**David Guzik** (Enduring Word): The four soldiers took His outer garments, each receiving one part. The tunic was seamless, woven from top to bottom — a valuable garment. The detail testifies to the eyewitness character of John’s account.

**Ellicott** adds that the seamless tunic (under-garment, reaching neck to feet) was unusual; ordinary tunics had two pieces clasped at the shoulder. He notes that priestly tunics were made in one piece (citing Josephus on Aaron’s tunic), suggesting a possible symbolic link to Jesus’ priestly office.

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html

---

### v. 24 — Casting lots for the tunic; fulfillment of Psalm 22:18.

**Guzik**: The soldiers unknowingly fulfilled prophecy. “As the Son of God died for the sins of the world men carelessly laughed and played games at His feet.”

**Gill** and **Ellicott** both note the quotation from Psalm 22:18 follows the Septuagint closely. **Ellicott** observes this is a classic instance of John showing Scripture fulfilled in events that the actors themselves did not intend as fulfillment.

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html

---

### v. 25 — The women standing near the cross.

**Ellicott** discusses whether three or four women are listed. The question is whether “His mother’s sister” is the same as “Mary the wife of Clopas.” The balance of evidence, he says, favours four women in two pairs: (1) His mother and her sister (possibly Salome, John’s own mother, whom John never names); (2) Mary the wife of Clopas and Mary Magdalene. The Peshito Syriac version (2nd century) inserted “and” after “sister,” supporting four women.

**Guzik**: “It is difficult to comprehend the agony of Mary as she saw her Son crucified. She was witness to the pain, humiliation, shame, suffering, and death of her Son.”

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/

---

### vv. 26–27 — “Woman, behold your son” / “Behold your mother.”

**Traditional reading (all sources agree)**: Jesus, even in extreme agony, made provision for His widowed mother by entrusting her to “the disciple whom He loved” (John). This fulfilled the fifth commandment and demonstrated filial piety. Joseph is presumed dead by this point.

**Guzik**: “Even in death Jesus remained others-centered… He did not cling to material possessions or demand pity.”

**Ellicott**: Jesus committed Mary to John rather than to His own “brethren” (half-brothers), who did not yet believe (cf. John 7:5). The language is “legal and quite similar to the terms used commonly in adoption proceedings” (citing Carson).

**Gill**: John “took her to his own home” — meaning into his own care and household. He adds that Jesus addressed her as “Woman” (Greek *gynai*), which was “an affectionate and respectful way of speaking to her,” not cold or distant (cf. John 2:4).

**Augustine** (Catholic Church Father, via New Advent): Augustine contrasts Jesus’ earlier words to Mary at Cana (“Woman, what have I to do with you? Mine hour is not yet come”) with this moment. Then, about to perform divine acts, He “repelled, as one unknown, her who was the mother, not of His divinity, but of His human infirmity.” Now, in human suffering, He “commended with human affection the mother by whom He had become man.” Augustine calls the cross “the very chair of office from which the Master was imparting instruction” about caring for parents. He also notes that John, having left all to follow Jesus, received the hundredfold promise (Mark 10:29-30) — Mary herself being part of that hundredfold blessing.

**Catholic reading** (catholic.com): Jesus’ entrusting Mary to John strongly suggests Mary had no other children. If she had, it would have been “an outrage of the highest order” in first-century Jewish culture to entrust her to an outsider. This supports the Catholic doctrine of Mary’s perpetual virginity.

**Constable** (Evangelical): Jesus’ act placed Mary under John’s authority, “a position that some Roman Catholics have found very uncomfortable in view of their doctrine of Mary’s supremacy.”

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/john-19.html
- URL: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701119.htm
- URL: https://www.catholic.com/bible-navigator/perpetual-virginity-of-mary/john1926-27

---

### v. 28 — “I am thirsty.”

**Guzik**: Jesus “knew that His great work, His life and death work on the cross was fulfilled.” He then prepared to yield His life. The cry “I thirst” was both a genuine expression of physical agony and a deliberate act to fulfill Scripture (Psalm 69:21).

**Ellicott** wrestles with the grammar: the Greek words for “accomplished” and “fulfilled” come from the same root (*teleō*). He suggests the meaning is “all things were now completed that the Scripture might be accomplished,” referring to the whole life of Jesus rather than only the words immediately following. He notes that Jesus had earlier refused the stupefying drink (Matthew 27:34) but now, with all things accomplished, He “seeks relief from the physical agony of the thirst caused by His wounds.”

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html

---

### v. 29 — Sour wine on hyssop.

**Ellicott**: The “vinegar” was the ordinary sour wine (*posca*) drunk by Roman soldiers. The vessel was placed near the cross for the crucified, since thirst was an expected accompaniment of crucifixion. The mention of “hyssop” is peculiar to John. Bochart identifies it as marjoram or a similar plant with stalks a foot to a foot-and-a-half high, sufficient to reach Jesus’ mouth on the cross. Hyssop appears also in Hebrews 9:19 and frequently in the Old Testament (e.g., Passover: Exodus 12:22), carrying sacrificial symbolism.

**Guzik**: The sponge on hyssop lifted to Jesus’ mouth was a final act of human “kindness” amid the cruelty.

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/

---

### v. 30 — “It is finished.” (*Tetelestai*)

This is the most theologically commented-upon verse in the passage.

**Guzik** (Pentecostal/Charismatic tradition): *Tetelestai* was “the cry of a winner.” It means “paid in full.” Jesus “had finished the eternal purpose of the cross. It stands today as a finished work, the foundation of all Christian peace and faith.” He cites Tenney that the verb *teleō* was used in receipts in the 1st–2nd centuries, meaning “paid in full.” Guzik also emphasizes that Jesus “bowed His head” — a peaceful act, like lying on a pillow, not hanging His head in defeat. He “gave up His spirit” voluntarily; death had no claim on a sinless man.

**Reformed reading (Ligonier / R.C. Sproul)**: “When He said, ‘It is finished,’ He was saying not just that His life was over but that His mission had been fulfilled. His purpose in coming to earth and going to the cross was accomplished.” Because Jesus accomplished redemption, “we can be confident that in Him, God sees us as righteous and worthy of His kingdom. We can rest in His grace, knowing that Jesus has paid for all of our sin.”

**Reformed Baptist (Desiring God / John Piper)**: Jesus “saw his task accomplished, his work complete, his Father’s will fulfilled.” Piper enumerates: “the law fulfilled, the devil disarmed, the cup of wrath drained, and sinners saved.” He stresses that “we cannot add to a finished work. We cannot contribute to completion. We can only hold out the hand of faith and humbly, happily receive it.” Yet Piper also insists that the Christian still has “a race to run, a devil to resist, good works to walk in, and holiness to pursue” but always “on finished ground.”

**Precept Austin** (Evangelical): Explains the perfect tense of *tetelestai*: “a PAST completed act with PRESENT effect.” Jesus’ sacrifice “may have occurred in time and space, but its results will last for eternity.” It notes that the divine self-satisfaction occurs only twice in Scripture: at Creation (“very good,” Genesis 1:31) and at Redemption (“It is finished,” John 19:30). Quoting Erwin Lutzer: “my sins are on Jesus, not on me. Yes, there is sin within me but not on me.”

**Ellicott**: Orders the Seven Words of the Cross: (1) “Father, forgive them”; (2) “Today… Paradise”; (3) “Woman, behold thy son”; (4) “My God, why have You forsaken Me?”; (5) “I thirst”; (6) “It is finished”; (7) “Into Thy hands I commend My spirit.” He notes that the bowing of the head is a detail “peculiar to St. John” — an eyewitness touch.

**GotQuestions.org** (Evangelical): *Tetelestai* is “an accounting term that means ‘paid in full.’” Jesus “was declaring the debt owed to His Father was wiped away completely and forever… Jesus eliminated the debt owed by mankind—the debt of sin.”

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/
- URL: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/redemption-accomplished
- URL: https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/finished
- URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/tetelestai-paid_in_full
- URL: https://www.gotquestions.org/it-is-finished.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html

---

### v. 31 — Day of Preparation; request for legs to be broken.

**Guzik**: The Jews wanted the bodies removed before sundown because the approaching Sabbath was a “high day” (the weekly Sabbath coinciding with Passover). Deuteronomy 21:22-23 required that a hanged body not remain overnight. Breaking the legs (*crurifragium*) hastened death because the crucified person could no longer push up to breathe.

**Ellicott**: The Roman custom was to leave bodies on the cross; the Jews considered this defilement (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). The “high day” refers to the Sabbath coinciding with the 15th of Nisan (the first day of the Feast), doubling its sanctity.

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html

---

### vv. 32–33 — Legs of the two criminals broken; Jesus’ legs not broken.

**Guzik**: The soldiers, experienced in crucifixion, “knew when a man had died and when he was still alive.” They saw Jesus was already dead and did not break His legs — fulfilling Psalm 34:20.

**Ellicott**: The purpose of *crurifragium* was to ensure death or prevent escape. Jesus had already “by His own will committed His spirit to His Father.”

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html

---

### v. 34 — Piercing of Jesus’ side; blood and water.

**Guzik**: “A random act from man’s perspective, yet it fulfilled the prophecies of Psalm 34:20 (no bones broken) and Zechariah 12:10 (pierced) with exact precision.”

**Ellicott**: Since the soldiers already knew Jesus was dead, the piercing was not to cause death but to “make death doubly sure.” The Greek word for “pierced” (*enyssen*) occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, but John 20:27 confirms it caused a deep wound that penetrated to the interior organs. If the soldier stood before the cross, the wound would naturally be in the left side.

**Constable** (Evangelical): “What led the soldier to pierce Jesus’ side with his spear is unclear and unimportant. Perhaps it was just another senseless act of brutality, or he may have wanted to see if he could get some reaction from Jesus.”

**Medical/historical note** (via Precept Austin / Dr. William Edwards): The flow of “blood and water” is consistent with what modern medicine would describe as the separation of blood into its components (clot and serum) after death, or the piercing of the pericardial sac around the heart releasing a watery fluid. This detail further confirms actual death.

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/john-19.html
- URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-19-commentary

---

### v. 35 — John’s eyewitness testimony.

**Guzik**: John “solemnly assures” his readers that he saw these events personally. The testimony is given “so that you also may believe” — the evangelistic purpose of the entire Gospel (John 20:31).

**Ellicott**: This verse is John’s parenthetical insertion, authenticating the account as that of an eyewitness. The emphatic “his testimony is true” underscores the reliability of the Fourth Gospel.

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html

---

### vv. 36–37 — Fulfillment of Scripture: no bone broken; they will look on the One pierced.

**Guzik**: Two prophecies fulfilled: (1) “Not one of His bones will be broken” — originally speaking of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12), also Psalm 34:20; (2) “They will look on the One they have pierced” — Zechariah 12:10, pointing to a future day when Israel will recognize their Messiah.

**Gill**: Connects the unbroken bones to the Passover lamb typology. Jesus is the true Passover Lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), and as such not a bone of Him was broken — exactly as the type required.

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/19.htm

---

### v. 38 — Joseph of Arimathea requests the body.

**Guzik**: Joseph was “a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jews.” God “raised up two previously secret disciples (Joseph and Nicodemus) to receive the body of Jesus.” Joseph’s action required courage: he went to Pilate publicly, identifying himself with a condemned man.

**Ellicott**: Only John notes that Joseph was a secret disciple. The Synoptics (Matthew 27:57-60; Mark 15:42-46; Luke 23:50-54) describe him as a rich member of the Sanhedrin who had not consented to their decision.

**Pett**: Joseph “being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Judaisers” — Pett uses “Judaisers” to translate *Ioudaioi*, reflecting the Johannine usage where “the Jews” often denotes the religious authorities rather than the people as a whole.

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/john-19.html

---

### v. 39 — Nicodemus brings myrrh and aloes (~75 pounds / 100 litrai).

**Guzik**: Nicodemus, who first came to Jesus by night (John 3:1-15), now steps forward publicly. The enormous quantity of spices (about 75 pounds / 34 kg) “reflected Nicodemus’ great respect for Jesus” and was a lavish, royal amount.

**Ellicott**: “Aloes” here is an Eastern odoriferous wood (sandalwood), not the medicinal aloe of commerce. Myrrh and aloes were pulverised and mixed. The quantity far exceeds what could be placed in the linen wrappings; part may have been placed in the sepulchre, as at the burial of King Asa (2 Chronicles 16:14).

**Constable**: Myrrh was a fragrant resin; aloes was powdered sandalwood. “The purpose of covering a corpse with this aromatic powder was to dry it out and to lessen the foul odor that putrefaction caused.”

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/john-19.html

---

### v. 40 — Wrapping the body in linen with spices, according to Jewish custom.

**Guzik**: They “bound it in strips of linen with the spices.” This was not Egyptian-style mummification but the Jewish burial custom of wrapping the body with cloths and aromatic spices.

**Constable**: The Jewish custom was to place the corpse on a long sheet, fold it over the head and back to the feet, tie the feet, and secure the arms with strips. A separate cloth covered the face (cf. John 11:44; 20:7). “John’s interest was not in the manner of the burial as much as the honor that Joseph and Nicodemus bestowed on Jesus.”

**Ellicott**: The same word does not occur as in Luke 24:12 for the linen cloths, but the manner is illustrated by John 11:44 (Lazarus’ burial).

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/john-19.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html

---

### v. 41 — The garden and the new tomb.

**Guzik**: The tomb was in a garden near Golgotha. It was new, “in which no one had yet been laid” — a detail noted also by Luke (23:53) and Matthew (27:60). Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a colt “whereon never man before had sat” (Mark 11:2) and was buried in a tomb “wherein never man before had lain” — “in all things He was ‘separate from sinners’” (Hebrews 7:26, as noted by the Pulpit Commentary / JFB).

**Ellicott**: John’s account makes the choice of the tomb depend on its nearness; the Synoptics make it depend on its belonging to Joseph. “The one account implies the other.” The burial required both that the tomb was at hand and that its owner was willing.

**Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges**: The tomb was probably Joseph’s own (Matthew 27:60), “hewn out in the rock.” The garden location recalls John 18:1 (the garden of Gethsemane) — Jesus’ passion began and ended in a garden.

**Pett**: “The mention of the unused tomb is to stress the importance of the One Who lay there. He was being treated as royalty. The thought may also be that it had not been defiled by death. Furthermore new, unused things were regularly used when God was seen as involved” (cf. 1 Samuel 6:7; 2 Samuel 6:3).

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-19.html
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/john-19.html
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-42.htm (Cambridge Bible, Poole, Pulpit excerpts)

---

### v. 42 — Laid there because of the Preparation Day and the tomb’s nearness.

**Guzik**: The burial was hurried because the Sabbath began at sundown. The nearby tomb was providential — without it, the burial preparations could not have been completed before the Sabbath.

**Cambridge Bible**: “It would seem as if the burial was hastily and temporarily performed. They probably intended after the Sabbath to make a more solemn and complete burial elsewhere.” Also notes that “the Jews’ preparation day” may be “another slight indication that the Gospel was written outside Palestine” or that by John’s time there was already a Christian “preparation day.”

**Matthew Poole**: “The Friday was so nearly at an end that they had not time to go to any distance, and therefore availed themselves of the neighbouring tomb as a provisional, if not permanent, resting-place.”

**Pett**: The burial “had to be accomplished quickly because of the coming Sabbath. But Joseph had this tomb conveniently near to the place of crucifixion.”

**Pulpit Commentary**: John assigns the reason for this specific tomb as the rapidity with which the burial could be completed, owing to its nearness. This is John’s third reference to the “Preparation” in this chapter (cf. v. 14, v. 31), underscoring the chronological framework of the passion.

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-19/
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/19-42.htm
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/john-19.html

## Summary of Protestant Traditions Compared

On the core meaning of this passage, Protestant traditions are largely unified — all affirm the historicity, the fulfillment of Scripture, the voluntary nature of Jesus’ death, and the finished work of atonement. Differences are modest:

- **Reformed (Ligonier/Sproul)**: Emphasise the finished work as the basis for imputed righteousness and rest in grace — nothing can be added.
- **Reformed Baptist (Desiring God/Piper)**: Strongly stress that good works, holiness, and spiritual warfare follow *from* finished ground, not as additions to it.
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik)**: Accent the victorious cry of *tetelestai* (“cry of a winner”), the voluntary surrender of the spirit, and the practical, relational example of Jesus caring for His mother.
- **Anglican (Ellicott)**: Focus on historical-grammatical detail, harmonisation with the Synoptics, and the eyewitness character of John’s narrative.
- **Lutheran and Methodist**: No specific Lutheran (LCMS, 1517.org) or Methodist/Wesleyan (Seedbed, wesley.nnu.edu) commentary on these exact verses was retrievable within search limits.

## Catholic and Orthodox Distinctives

- **Mary as Mother of the Church**: Augustine and Catholic interpreters (catholic.com, newadvent.org) read John 19:26-27 as more than filial provision. The “beloved disciple” represents all believers; Jesus gives Mary as mother to the Church and the Church to Mary. Augustine describes the cross as the “chair of office” from which the Master taught.
- **Perpetual Virginity**: Catholic teaching (catholic.com) argues that Jesus’ entrusting Mary to John implies she had no other children, since it would be culturally unthinkable in first-century Judaism to entrust one’s mother to an outsider if biological sons existed.
- **Blood and Water as Sacraments**: Catholic tradition (noted in broader reading but not directly retrieved for this passage) reads the blood and water from Jesus’ side as symbolising the Eucharist and Baptism, the two chief sacraments flowing from Christ’s death. (This is referenced in Catholic tradition, e.g., the Catechism, though the specific page could not be retrieved.)
